title: Birbal's Khichdi
text:
On a bitter winter day, the emperor Akbar wondered aloud whether anyone would stand all night in icy water for money. He announced a reward for any man who could do it. A poor man came forward, stood through the night in a freezing lake, and in the morning came to the court to claim his prize.

Akbar asked him how he had endured the cold. The man answered that he had kept his eyes on a lamp burning far away in a window of the palace. At once the emperor declared that the lamp had warmed him, so he had not really met the challenge, and sent him away without the reward.

Birbal, Akbar's witty minister, said nothing. The next day he did not come to court. The emperor sent for him and was told that Birbal was cooking khichdi, a dish of rice and lentils, and would come when it was ready. Hours passed. At last Akbar went to see for himself. He found Birbal sitting beside a small fire, with the pot hanging from a branch high above the flames.

When Akbar laughed and asked how food could cook so far from the fire, Birbal asked how a man in a lake could be warmed by a lamp half a mile away. Akbar understood, called back the poor man and paid him in full.
lesson: If you find yourself searching for a technicality to avoid paying what you owe, apply the same reasoning to yourself. When someone shows you the flaw, have the grace to correct it.
caveat: Birbal was a real minister at Akbar's court, but the witty tales about him are folklore, not historical records.
